planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring once frost danger has passed, in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Fe is self-fruitful and needs no separate pollinator tree.

directions: Santa Fe originated in Santa Fe Springs, California, and is prized as a hermaphroditic carob that sets regular, heavy crops entirely on its own without a male tree nearby. The open-habited tree carries slender, reddish twigs and leaves with 8 to 10 leaflets, and produces long pods, 8 to 10 inches, with sugar content around 47 percent. It suits coastal and foothill climates especially well, tolerating poor and rocky soil once established while needing only occasional deep watering. Harvest in early autumn when pods have dried and turned fully brown on the tree.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; Casuda is a female selection and needs a male or hermaphroditic carob nearby for pollination.

directions: Casuda is a long-established female carob cultivar from Valencia, Spain, grown commercially for its flat, medium-length pods that run unusually high in sugar, often cited near 56 percent. The vigorous, upright tree needs a male or self-fruitful cultivar planted within range to set fruit reliably. Like other carobs it thrives in hot, dry, Mediterranean-type conditions and tolerates thin, rocky, alkaline soils poorly suited to most fruit trees. Pick pods in early to mid autumn once they have dried and turned dark brown, when the seeds inside rattle.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Tylliria is a female cultivar that needs a male or hermaphroditic carob nearby to produce pods.

directions: Tylliria is Cyprus's leading commercial carob, a vigorous, upright female selection with reddish twigs and large leaves, grown there for export and widely used for milling into carob flour. Its pods are dark mahogany-brown, slightly curved, and run around a foot long, with sugar content regularly exceeding 48 percent. The tree needs a pollinator planted nearby and performs best in full sun with excellent drainage, surviving drought far better than most temperate fruit trees once its roots are established. Harvest pods in autumn once fully dried and dark on the tree.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; check with the nursery on Badan's pollination needs before deciding whether a second carob tree is required.

directions: Badan was selected in La Jolla, California by noted carob breeder Paul H. Thomson and is grown for its dark brown pods of notably high quality. Like other coastal California carob selections, it is well suited to mild, dry Mediterranean-type climates and struggles in humid or waterlogged sites. The tree is slow to establish but long-lived and drought-hardy once mature, requiring little input beyond occasional deep watering during pod fill. Harvest pods in autumn once they have dried and darkened fully on the tree.

common_name: Hwang Kum #3 Che (Large Early-Ripening Korean Mandarin Melon Berry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil, watering regularly through the first season; Hwang Kum #3 ripens earlier than most che selections, widening the window for a full harvest in shorter-season gardens.

directions: Hwang Kum #3 is a modern Korean che selection bred for unusually large fruit that ripens earlier in the season than older che cultivars, giving growers in cooler zones a better chance of a finished crop before fall frost. As with other che, left untrained the tree grows into a large thorny multi-stemmed form, so most growers prune to a single leader or graft onto Osage orange rootstock for a more manageable tree shape. Being a female selection it needs a male che or pollen source nearby to set its sweet, maroon-red, bumpy-skinned fruit. Plant in full sun with consistent moisture during the growing season for the best fruit size and yield.
